steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise comparison of DNA and RNA:

1. Chemical Structure  
   • Sugar  
     – DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
     – RNA: Ribose (has an –OH group on the 2′ carbon)  
   • Nitrogenous Bases  
     – DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
     – RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces Thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
   • Strands  
     – DNA: Typically double-stranded helix, complementary strands held by hydrogen bonds  
     – RNA: Typically single-stranded, can fold into complex 3D shapes  

2. Function  
   • DNA  
     – Long-term storage of genetic information  
     – Template for its own replication during cell division  
     – Template for RNA synthesis (transcription)  
   • RNA  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) & ribosomal RNA (rRNA): play central roles in protein synthesis  
     – Regulatory RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA) and catalytic RNAs (ribozymes)  

3. Cellular Location  
   • DNA  
     – Eukaryotes: confined to the nucleus (and mitochondria/plastids)  
     – Prokaryotes: in the nucleoid region of the cytoplasm  
   • RNA  
     – Synthesized in nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes)  
     – Functions mainly in the cytoplasm (ribosomes, regulatory complexes)  

4. Stability and Lifespan  
   • DNA  
     – Highly stable under physiological conditions  
     – Long half-life; ideal for permanent information storage  
   • RNA  
     – Less chemically stable (2′–OH can promote strand cleavage)  
     – Rapid turnover—allows dynamic regulation of gene expression  

5. Replication and Turnover  
   • DNA  
     – Replicates once per cell cycle via DNA polymerases  
     – Proofreading and repair mechanisms maintain fidelity  
   • RNA  
     – Transcribed “on demand” by RNA polymerases  
     – No extensive proofreading; short-lived, enabling quick response to cellular needs  

Summary  
DNA is the stable, double-stranded molecule that stores and preserves the genome. RNA is a more versatile, single-stranded molecule that takes genetic information from DNA and uses it to build and regulate proteins and other cellular processes.
